Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette: Tuan Nguyen had kept the memory of that November evening suspended for decades, not as a clear picture but as a distant echo that sometimes slipped into the room without warning. He was forty-two when his wife struck him during a heated argument in their dimly lit kitchen. He remembered the sudden arc of her arm, the sharp crack of his shoulder against the cabinet, and the way the overhead light had flickered out, leaving him pinned beneath the heavy oak table. What frightened him most was not the pain but the absolute certainty that another blow would follow. When he recalled it now, the terror he felt at the time rose through him as though it were happening again, and his body automatically settled into the same rigid posture: knees drawn up, shoulders hunched, hands braced against the floorboards. He would look at the memory and feel it belonged to a stranger, a man trapped in that darkened kitchen, while he remained firmly in his present body. Over the months that followed, the household grew heavier. He found himself jumpy in his own kitchen, every creak of the floorboards sending a quick flash of alert through his chest. When he later took up work as a nanny, caring for a family’s children in their suburban home, the environment only multiplied these sensations. He was unable to relax even in the quiet nursery, where the air was warm and the baby gates secured. An unexpected movement nearby—a toddler rolling across the rug, a cat leaping from the windowsill—drew him to react as if he were in danger, his breath catching and his muscles tightening before he could name the source. He had come to believe that the world was full of sudden arrivals, and he kept his gaze fixed on the periphery, watching for the next unpredictable shift. He had not allowed himself to feel or express anger, burying any rising frustration beneath a quiet compliance. When the children demanded too much or the parents left tight schedules behind them, he simply stepped back, avoiding anything that could be stressful. The dark circumstances of his past slowly drew him toward avoidance. He began taking the children on early afternoon walks, steering clear of the evening hours when the house shadows lengthened and the dining room lamp cast long, sharp angles across the floor. He avoided the basement playroom, the dimmed theater, and even the car at night, moving through these spaces with deliberate care. Over weeks and months, these habits accumulated. He declined evening shift cover, took longer lunch breaks, and found that his professional life narrowed to daylight hours. He remains married to his wife of many years, though she noticed how he would sit just beyond the reach of the overhead lamp, shoulders squared as though bracing for a familiar pressure. Now, at seventy-two, Tuan sits in his sunlit apartment, folding the children’s laundry with steady, methodical hands. His PCL-5 score of 57 reflects a quiet accumulation of vigilance, but it is the lingering stillness that draws him to the clinic. He has come to seek help because the memories no longer stay distant; they slip into his shoulders and stiffen his neck, and he wonders whether the fear of being trapped under that table has outlived its usefulness. He is most hopeful for a way to let the body uncoil without demanding he explain itself, and he fears, above all, that he will continue to watch the shadows for a blow that no longer comes.
